title: Economic policy experts, whistleblower urge House to oppose captive insurance tax pause
summary: Economic policy advocates don’t want to see Maryland’s hospitals let “off the hook” for what could be years of unpaid taxes on offshore insurance accounts, calling on lawmakers to abandon a plan to pause collections on those taxes.
content:
by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters April 9, 2026

by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters April 9, 2026

Economic policy advocates don’t want to see Maryland’s hospitals let “off the hook” for what could be years of unpaid taxes on offshore insurance accounts, calling on lawmakers to abandon a plan to pause collections on those taxes.

In an attempt to settle an ongoing dispute over whether nonprofit hospitals should have been paying taxes for what’s known as “captive insurance” sheltered in the Cayman Islands, the Senate last month agreed to put collection of the tax on hold for two years while the Maryland Insurance Administration studied the issue.

But critics told the House Ways and Means Committee on Wednesday that the compromise, contained in Senate Bill 890, could open the door for hospitals to escape paying state taxes on out-of-state insurance premiums, particularly since it does not say whether hospitals will be required to pay any taxes owed once the study is completed.

“Our preference would be that this bill does not pass — that the MIA be able to go ahead with its process of being able to investigate this and collect the taxes owed,” Kali Schumitz with Maryland Center on Economic Policy, told the committee. “We’re particularly concerned also about the moratorium and the precedent it sets — a company going years not paying taxes that they owed and just getting let off the hook with no penalty.

Senate eyes pause on collection of tax on hospitals’ offshore ‘captive’ insurance

Marceline White, executive director for the Economic Action Maryland Fund, agreed that SB 890 is “silent on whether at the end of that two-year moratorium, hospitals would have to pay the back taxes that they owe.”

“There’s huge fiscal implications at a very difficult time for the state,” said White, adding that the bill needs to be rewritten or should just die.

At issue is what’s known as “captive insurance,” which is when a company forms its own insurance company — a captive — to help cover claim not covered by commercial insurance. For hospitals, that may be the costs of medical malpractice claims or cybersecurity risks, for example.

Maryland does not have a regulatory framework to let companies establish captives within the state. So decades ago, Maryland nonprofit hospitals set up captives in offshore locations such as the Cayman Islands, hospital representatives testified earlier this year.

Some nonprofits paid taxes on their captive plans, but most hospitals believed they were not subject to the tax, raising questions about whether they were dodging the tax or the MIA should have been more active in collecting it.

SB 890, sponsored by Sen. Dawn Gile (D-Anne Arundel), originally carved out nonprofit hospitals from the tax entirely. That was quickly amended to clarify that they would be required to pay that tax going forward, but they would not have to pay back any missed state taxes for captives.

After continued pushback, Gile amended the bill on the Senate floor to pause the tax collection completely for two years while MIA studies the issue. But that raised even more concerns from people who believe hospitals are required to pay the tax.

Jason Schupp, the whistleblower largely responsible for the awareness of nonprofit hospitals using captive insurance, says that as much as $3 billion of nonprofit hospital funds are sitting in those offshore captives. Schupp, who had been largely anonymous so far, decided to testify in the open Wednesday to answer lawmakers’ questions on the complex issue.

“I am here today to talk about how captives exploit state premium taxes,” Schupp told Ways and Means. “These are for-profit, Cayman Island insurance companies that are not registered with the United States … there is – we don’t know if it’s $1.7 billion or $3 billion – of Maryland money sitting in the Cayman Islands that is completely invisible to you.”

Some committee members believed there was enough ambiguity in the law to warrant a pause on the tax to get to the bottom of it.

“I think we have a lot of questions to answer, and I think this study would definitely be the way to look at it,” said Del. Robert B. Long (R-Baltimore County). “Let’s get some final answers and let’s hopefully come up with a situation or come up with an answer.”

But Del. Joe Vogel (D-Montgomery) argued that the hospitals can and should pay the tax.

“This is where I struggle to have sympathy (for hospitals),” he . “There are costs that can very quickly add up … sure, it might mean that CEO salaries are a little lower next year. It might mean you have to spend a little less on lobbying.”

With just days left i legislative session, delegates will have to move fast on the bill if they want to address the issue this year. And since the bill was jointly assigned in the House — to Way and Means and to the Health Committee — both will need to approve the legislation before it goes to the floor for full House consideration.

Any House changes to SB 890 would need to go back to the Senate for the Senate for approval.

Ways and Means Chair Jheanelle Wilkins (D-Montgomery) could also decide not to bring the bill up for a vote, letting the bill die in committee. She did not indicate Wednesday which way she might be leaning.

“This is a very unusual bill. It’s also an unusual subject matter for the Ways and Means Committee,” Wilkins said. “There’s a lot to look at with this legislation.”
